title: The bow drops (1.40–1.47)
hook: the last argument, the last verse of chapter one, and a warrior sitting down in the middle of the field

segments.voice: Yesterday, I see no good in killing my kin: Arjuna's case against the war, heard in full. Your line was the honest objection. Did you let someone finish? Today, the end of chapter one. Day one hundred sixty.

There's a moment some people know too well. You've been holding it together for weeks. You've made all your arguments, to yourself and to everyone else. And then, one ordinary afternoon, in a parking lot or the kitchen or the office bathroom, you just sit down. Not because you decided to. Because you can't stand up anymore. That's where chapter one of the Gita ends. Not with a battle. With the best warrior on the field sitting down in his chariot, and his bow on the floor.
screen: `WEEKS OF HOLDING IT TOGETHER.` → `YOU JUST SIT DOWN.` → `THE BOW ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Arjuna's last arguments, in verses forty to forty-four, are about what a war like this destroys beyond the dead. When a family is wiped out, he says, its old ways die with it: the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together. Chaos follows, and the generations after are lost. It's the argument of a man from his own time and world, and people read it differently today; some commentators hear in it a real grief for everything a war erases, and some hear a mind grabbing any argument it can find. Either way, it ends in a cry. Alas, he says, we're about to commit a great wrong, killing our own people out of greed for a kingdom. Then the saddest line in the chapter. It would be better for me, he says, if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle, unarmed and not fighting back. And then Sanjaya, telling the blind king, describes what he sees. In Sanskrit: visrijya sasharam chapam shoka samvigna manasah. Casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind shaken with grief. Arjuna sinks down onto the seat of his chariot, there between the two armies. That's the end of chapter one. And here's the surprise. Every chapter of the Gita has a title calling it a yoga, a path. This one is called Arjuna Vishada Yoga. The yoga of Arjuna's despair. Despair, counted as a path. Nothing that follows, none of Krishna's teaching, happens without this. The book begins because a man sat down and said, I can't.
screen: `WHAT A WAR ERASES.` · `BETTER IF THEY KILLED ME UNARMED.` · `HE CASTS ASIDE HIS BOW.` · `THE YOGA OF DESPAIR.` · then, large: `THE BOOK BEGINS WITH I CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put the bow down. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been carrying and fighting with for too long. Picture it as a bow, heavy in your hands, arrows on your back. Now, without making any decision about tomorrow, just set it down beside you. Let your hands be empty. Sit down, the way Arjuna sits in his chariot, right in the middle of everything. You don't have to fix anything yet. Saying I can't, honestly, is the start of the book. The bell holds the time.
The bow drops. The last verse of chapter one: Arjuna casts aside his bow and arrows and sits down, his mind shaken with grief.
Your line: I can't. Today, if something's too much, say so plainly to one person you trust. That's where help begins. Day one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Chapter one of the Gita is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair; many readers and teachers treat Arjuna's collapse at 1.47 as the necessary starting point for the teaching that follows.

what it means: the hero reaches the end of himself, and says so. the teaching can't begin until he does.
what a scholar hears: the chapter colophons call each chapter a yoga; the first is vishada yoga, despair itself counted as a path.

notes: 1.40–1.44 include Arjuna's argument about the corruption of women of the family and varnasankara (mixing of varnas), and ancestors falling without pinda offerings. The script summarizes this as 'the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together' and does not spell out the women/varna content. A Keeper should decide whether to name it explicitly.
'Some commentators hear real grief... some hear a mind grabbing any argument' is the script's summary of differing readings. Confirm.
Chapter colophon titles vary slightly across editions (Arjuna Vishada Yoga is standard). Confirm.
Gita 1.47 in some editions is numbered 1.46. Confirm.
